stances.claim: The Panganiban formula in Veterans reflected distortions already present in RA 7941 -- it did not create them; Veterans itself suggested Congress revise the law.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-defense of own jurisprudence (distortions were legislative, not judicial)

stances.claim: Banat's voiding of the 2% threshold produced a more distorted result than Veterans -- 55 winners vs 22 -- because it abandoned proportional representation while retaining the 3-seat limit.

Amending RA 7941 is no longer viable because dominant solons who benefited will block it -- only a constitutional convention (not a constituent assembly of Congress) can fix or abolish the party-list.
stances.rhetorical_move: conflict-of-interest disqualification of Congress from self-reform

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban takes up the second major party-list question -- how many seats -- by tracing the evolution from the 'Panganiban formula' in Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (October 6, 2000, which he wrote for a 12-3 majority) through to Banat v. Comelec (2009). Veterans mandated four inviolable parameters: 20% ceiling, 2% threshold, 3-seat limit, and proportional representation -- producing 22 winners. Banat voided the 2% threshold to chase the 20% ceiling, awarding 55 winners instead, but retained the 3-seat cap while abandoning proportional representation, creating absurdities like Buhay Party (7.33% of votes, 3 seats) and Cocofed (0.98%, 1 seat), with the theoretical possibility of a 10,000-vote party winning a seat. Combined with the reversal of the 'marginalized and underrepresented' doctrine, the rich and dynasties now dominate the 'mongrelized party-list system.' Statutory amendment is foreclosed -- the dominant beneficiaries will block it -- so CJ argues only a constitutional convention (not a constituent assembly) can either abolish the party-list or institute the necessary reforms.
